reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: Caused by deficient ferrochelatase, the final enzyme of haem biosynthesis; a phenotypically similar X-linked form results from gain-of-function ALAS2 mutations
Typically presents in early childhood with immediate painful, burning photosensitivity on sun exposure, often without prominent visible skin lesions
Acute reactions cause intense stinging or burning pain, erythema and oedema; chronic changes include waxy thickening and shallow scars over the knuckles and nose
The characteristic pain without blistering distinguishes it from the bullous cutaneous porphyrias and often leads to years of diagnostic delay
The biochemical hallmark is markedly raised free (metal-free) erythrocyte protoporphyrin, with normal urinary porphyrins because protoporphyrin is not water-soluble
A minority develop protoporphyric hepatopathy, as excess protoporphyrin is excreted in bile and can precipitate as gallstones or cause cholestatic liver failure
Management centres on strict sunlight and visible-light avoidance and photoprotection; afamelanotide is an approved treatment to increase light tolerance
reference.pathophysiology: Erythropoietic protoporphyria results from reduced activity of ferrochelatase, the last enzyme of haem biosynthesis, which inserts iron into protoporphyrin IX to form haem; in the X-linked variant, increased ALAS2 activity overproduces protoporphyrin. Either mechanism causes accumulation of lipophilic, photoreactive protoporphyrin, chiefly in erythrocytes. On exposure to visible light of the appropriate wavelength, protoporphyrin in dermal blood vessels generates reactive oxygen species that cause an acute, painful phototoxic reaction. Because protoporphyrin is water-insoluble it is cleared in bile rather than urine, and biliary overload can lead to gallstones and, in a minority, progressive cholestatic liver disease.
additionalDifferentials: Polymorphic light eruption and solar urticaria
Porphyria cutanea tarda and other bullous porphyrias
Secondary protoporphyrinaemia from lead poisoning or iron deficiency
additionalInvestigations: Erythrocyte protoporphyrin measurement, distinguishing free (metal-free) from zinc-bound protoporphyrin
Plasma fluorescence scanning with a characteristic emission peak
Molecular genetic testing of the FECH gene (and ALAS2 for the X-linked form)
Liver function tests and monitoring for protoporphyric hepatopathy
Iron studies, as iron status can influence the phenotype
Abdominal imaging where gallstones or hepatic involvement are suspected
redFlags: Signs of protoporphyric liver disease such as jaundice, rising bilirubin or hepatic failure
Rapidly worsening photosensitivity suggesting deteriorating liver function
Severe, disabling phototoxic pain limiting daily activity
reference.prognosis: Most patients have a normal lifespan with a chronic burden of painful photosensitivity; the main serious risk is the small proportion who develop rapidly progressive protoporphyric liver failure requiring specialist and sometimes transplant management.
pitfalls: Long diagnostic delay because painful photosensitivity without blistering is not recognised as porphyria
Relying on urinary porphyrins, which are normal, and missing the diagnosis
Overlooking progressive liver disease until it is advanced
Failing to protect the skin and eyes from visible as well as ultraviolet light
Not screening relatives, as inheritance and the low-expression FECH allele complicate risk assessment
references: Scriver's Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease
